categories.name: Fire
categories.description: Learn different methods for safely building a fire outdoors.

skills.name: Teepee Fire
skills.description: The teepee fire is a simple fire structure that allows heat and flames to rise through the center.
steps: Place dry tinder in the center.
Arrange small sticks around the tinder in a teepee shape.
Leave a small opening so air can reach the fire.
Light the tinder.
Add larger pieces of wood as the fire grows.
skills.imageAlt: Teepee fire structure made with kindling around a small fire

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: A teepee fire uses small pieces of wood arranged in a cone shape around tinder. The structure leaves open spaces that allow air to reach the fire.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: This structure can be useful when starting a campfire because small pieces of wood can catch fire before larger pieces are added.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: Tinder is placed in the center. Small dry sticks are placed around the tinder in a cone shape. Larger pieces of wood can be added after the fire becomes stronger.

skills.safety: Only build a fire where fires are allowed. Keep the area around the fire clear and never leave a burning fire unattended.

skills.name: Log Cabin Fire
skills.description: The log cabin fire uses stacked wood to create a stable and long-lasting fire.
steps: Place tinder and small kindling in the center.
Place two pieces of wood parallel to each other.
Add two more pieces across the first two.
Continue stacking the wood in alternating directions.
Light the tinder in the center.
skills.imageAlt: Log cabin fire structure with stacked pieces of firewood

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: The wood is arranged in a square shape. Each layer is placed across the layer below it, similar to the walls of a small log cabin.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: This structure can be used for a campfire when a stable arrangement of firewood is wanted.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: Two pieces of wood are placed parallel to each other. Another two pieces are placed across them. More layers can then be added while leaving space for air.

skills.safety: Use established fire areas when available. Keep water nearby and completely extinguish the fire before leaving the area.

skills.name: Lean-To Fire
skills.description: The lean-to fire protects a small flame and is useful when there is some wind.
steps: Place a large stick or log on the ground.
Put tinder next to the log.
Lean small sticks over the tinder against the log.
Light the tinder.
Add larger sticks as the fire grows.
skills.imageAlt: Lean-to fire structure with small sticks leaning against a larger log

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: A larger piece of wood is placed on the ground. Smaller sticks are leaned against it with tinder placed underneath.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: It is a simple fire structure that can provide support for small pieces of kindling while a fire is being started.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: Tinder is placed next to the larger piece of wood. Small sticks lean over the tinder. More wood can be added carefully after the fire begins burning.

skills.safety: Never build a fire where it is prohibited. Keep the fire small and under control and completely extinguish it when finished.

skills.name: Star Fire
skills.description: The star fire uses several logs pointing toward a small fire in the center.
steps: Build a small fire in the center.
Place several logs around it like the points of a star.
Push the ends of the logs toward the flames.
Move the logs inward as they burn.
Keep the center of the fire clear enough for airflow.
skills.imageAlt: Star fire with logs pointing toward a burning center

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: Several logs are placed on the ground with one end of each log pointing toward the center. From above, the arrangement looks like a star.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: The arrangement allows wood to be moved toward the center as the ends burn.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: A small fire is started in the center. The ends of the larger pieces of wood are positioned near the flame and can be moved inward carefully as they burn.

skills.safety: Keep the fire within an established fire area when possible. Never leave it unattended and completely extinguish it before leaving.

categories.name: Shelter
categories.description: Learn basic ways to create protection from weather and outdoor conditions.

skills.name: Lean-To Shelter
skills.description: A lean-to is a simple shelter made by leaning branches against a strong support.
steps: Find a strong tree or support.
Place a long branch against the support.
Lean smaller branches against the main branch.
Cover the structure with leaves and other natural material.
Make the covering thick enough to provide protection.
skills.imageAlt: Lean-to survival shelter made from branches

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: A lean-to shelter has a roof that slopes from a higher support down toward the ground. The roof can be covered with available materials to provide protection.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: A lean-to can provide basic protection from wind, light rain, and direct sunlight when spending time outdoors.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: A strong horizontal support is used as the main part of the shelter. Smaller branches can lean against it to create the roof. The roof can then be covered.

skills.safety: Check the area before building. Avoid dead trees, unstable branches, flood areas, and other possible hazards.

skills.name: Tarp Shelter
skills.description: A tarp shelter provides quick protection from rain, wind, and sun.
steps: Choose two strong trees or supports.
Tie a rope between them.
Place the tarp over the rope.
Secure the corners of the tarp to the ground.
Make sure the tarp is tight enough to shed rain.
skills.imageAlt: Tarp survival shelter secured between trees

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: A tarp shelter uses a waterproof sheet supported by trees, poles, or other strong anchor points.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: It can provide temporary protection from rain, wind, or direct sunlight while outdoors.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: A tarp is secured above the ground using cord and strong anchor points. It can be angled so rainwater runs away from the sheltered area.

skills.safety: Make sure the shelter is securely attached. Do not place it under dead branches or in areas where water may collect.

skills.name: Debris Hut
skills.description: A debris hut uses branches, leaves, and other natural materials for insulation.
steps: Create a strong ridge pole.
Lean branches along both sides.
Cover the branches with leaves and debris.
Add a thick layer for insulation.
Leave a small opening for entering the shelter.
skills.imageAlt: Debris hut made from branches and forest materials

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: A debris hut uses branches to create a basic frame. Leaves and other dry natural materials can cover the frame.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: It can provide basic protection when a normal tent or tarp is not available.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: A strong branch forms the main support. Smaller branches are placed along the sides. Dry leaves and other debris can then cover the frame.

skills.safety: Check the location for hazards before building. Avoid unstable trees, falling branches, animal areas, and places that may flood.

skills.name: Snow Shelter
skills.description: A snow shelter can provide protection from cold temperatures and wind.
steps: Choose an area with deep and stable snow.
Build or locate a large pile of snow.
Carefully create a protected interior space.
Keep the walls thick for insulation.
Make sure the shelter has proper ventilation.
skills.imageAlt: Emergency survival shelter built from snow

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: A snow shelter is a temporary structure that uses snow as part of its walls or covering. Snow can help block wind and provide insulation.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: Snow shelters are associated with cold and snowy environments where protection from wind and cold is important.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: Snow is shaped or dug to create a protected space. The exact design depends on the snow, weather, location, and available equipment.

skills.safety: Snow shelters can collapse and poor ventilation can be dangerous. Cold-weather shelter building requires proper knowledge and careful conditions.

categories.name: Water
categories.description: Learn basic methods for collecting and making water safer outdoors.

skills.name: Boiling Water
skills.description: Boiling is one of the simplest methods for treating water outdoors.
steps: Collect the clearest water available.
Filter out visible dirt and debris if necessary.
Place the water in a heat-safe container.
Bring the water to a rolling boil.
Allow the water to cool before drinking.
skills.imageAlt: Water boiling in a metal camping pot over a fire

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: Boiling uses high heat to kill many disease-causing microorganisms that may be present in water.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: Boiling can be used when the safety of available water is uncertain and a safe heat source is available.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: If the water is cloudy, it should first be allowed to settle and be filtered through a clean cloth when possible. The water can then be brought to a rolling boil before being allowed to cool.

sources.label: CDC - Making Water Safe in an Emergency

skills.safety: Boiling does not remove every type of chemical contamination. Avoid water that may contain fuel, toxic chemicals, or other dangerous pollutants.

skills.name: Filtering Water
skills.description: Filtering can remove dirt and other particles from collected water.
steps: Collect water in a clean container.
Use a proper outdoor water filter when available.
Follow the instructions for the filter.
Collect the filtered water in another clean container.
Use additional purification when necessary.
skills.imageAlt: Portable water filter being used beside a mountain stream

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: Water filtering passes water through a filter designed to remove certain particles and microorganisms.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: A portable water filter can be useful while hiking or camping when treated drinking water is not available.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: Water passes through the filter before it reaches a clean container. Different filters remove different contaminants, so the manufacturer's instructions are important.

sources.label: CDC - Making Water Safe in an Emergency

skills.safety: Not every filter removes viruses, chemicals, or all other contaminants. Use a filter designed for the situation and follow its instructions.

skills.name: Collecting Rainwater
skills.description: Rainwater can be collected using a clean surface and container.
steps: Find a clean container.
Place a tarp or another clean surface where it can catch rain.
Angle the surface toward the container.
Allow the rainwater to collect.
Treat the collected water before drinking when necessary.
skills.imageAlt: Rainwater being collected from a tarp into a container

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: Rainwater collection means catching rain and directing it into a container for later use.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: It may provide an additional source of water when rain is available and normal water supplies are limited.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: A clean tarp or similar surface can direct falling rain toward a clean container. The collected water should be protected from additional contamination.

sources.label: CDC - Finding Clean Water in an Emergency

skills.safety: Rainwater is not automatically safe to drink. It can collect germs and chemicals from the air or collection surface. Treat water when necessary before drinking it.

skills.name: Solar Still
skills.description: A solar still uses heat from the sun to collect a small amount of condensed water.
steps: Dig a hole in an area that receives sunlight.
Place a container in the center.
Cover the hole with clear plastic.
Place a small weight over the center of the plastic.
Allow condensation to drip into the container.
skills.imageAlt: Solar still collecting water using clear plastic and a container

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: A solar still is a simple system where heat causes moisture to evaporate. The water vapor then condenses on a surface and can be collected.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: It can demonstrate one way that water can move through evaporation and condensation when sunlight is available.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: Sunlight warms moisture inside a covered area. Water evaporates and reaches the cooler covering. It then condenses into droplets that can move toward a collection container.

skills.safety: A small solar still may produce very little water and should not be depended on as the only source of drinking water.

categories.name: Navigation
categories.description: Learn methods that can help you navigate or signal for assistance outdoors.

skills.name: Using a Compass
skills.description: A compass helps determine direction and can help you follow a planned route.
steps: Hold the compass flat in your hand.
Allow the compass needle to settle.
Identify north using the compass needle.
Determine the direction you need to travel.
Regularly check your direction while moving.
skills.imageAlt: Compass being used for navigation in the wilderness

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: A basic magnetic compass has a needle that aligns with Earth's magnetic field. This helps the user identify magnetic north and other directions.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: A compass can be useful while hiking, camping, or navigating an unfamiliar area, especially when used together with a map.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: The compass should be held flat and away from objects that may interfere with it. The needle helps identify direction, which can then be compared with a map or route.

skills.safety: Learn how to use a compass before depending on it outdoors. Electronic devices and some metal objects can also affect compass readings.

skills.name: Trail Markers
skills.description: Trail markers can help hikers identify and follow established routes.
steps: Look for official trail signs or painted markers.
Pay attention to the color and shape of markers.
Check markers regularly while traveling.
Avoid leaving the marked trail unnecessarily.
Turn back if you cannot confidently identify the route.
skills.imageAlt: Examples of trail markers used for outdoor navigation

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: Trail markers are signs, symbols, posts, or painted markings placed along established trails to help people follow a route.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: Pay attention to trail markers when hiking on marked trails, especially near turns, intersections, and changes in the route.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: Hikers follow the official markings for their selected trail. A map can also help confirm the route and important locations.

skills.safety: Do not create or change official trail markers. Stay on established trails when required and follow signs from park or land officials.

skills.name: Signal Fire
skills.description: A signal fire can help rescuers identify your location during an emergency.
steps: Choose an open location where the signal can be seen.
Clear flammable material away from the fire area.
Build and safely light a controlled fire.
Create visible smoke when signaling is necessary.
Never leave the fire unattended.
skills.imageAlt: Signal fire producing visible smoke in a wilderness clearing

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: A signal fire is intended to make a person's location more noticeable from a distance. The visible flame or smoke may attract attention.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: It may be considered during an emergency when signaling for rescue is necessary and local conditions allow a fire to be used safely.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: The main purpose is visibility. A signal should be placed where it can be noticed without creating a wildfire or another hazard.

sections.heading: Materials Needed
items: Water or another way to extinguish the fire

sources.label: National Park Service - Wildland Fire Safety

skills.safety: Fire can spread quickly. Follow local fire restrictions and never start a fire when conditions make it unsafe. Other signaling methods should be used when fire is prohibited.

skills.name: Ground Signals
skills.description: Large ground signals can make your location easier to see from the air.
steps: Choose a large open area.
Use rocks, branches, or other visible materials.
Create a large and simple emergency symbol.
Make the symbol contrast with the surrounding ground.
Keep the signal visible while waiting for assistance.
skills.imageAlt: Examples of large emergency ground signals

sections.heading: What It Is
paragraphs: A ground signal is a large marking created in an open area using materials that contrast with the surrounding ground.

sections.heading: When to Use It
paragraphs: Ground signals may be useful when trying to make your location more visible to rescuers from a distance.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: Materials can be arranged into a large, simple shape in a clear area. The signal should be large enough to stand out from the surrounding landscape.

skills.safety: Do not put yourself in danger while making a signal. Avoid cliffs, unstable ground, moving water, and other hazardous areas.
